newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian shares fall, trade seen slow, prices down.
newsitem.headline: Russian shares fall, trade seen slow, prices down.

text.p: Leading shares fell sharply on Thursday afternoon on news Russian President Boris Yeltsin had agreed to a heart operation at the end of the month but dealers widened spreads on most shares and daily losses were small.

Deals for bellwether Mosenergo dropped to $0.96 at close from $0.995 at 1314 GMT, shortly after the news broke, and $1.01 at Wednesday's close. LUKoil fell to $9.40 from $9.84 at 1314 and $9.85 on Wednesday.
"The thing's gone down, everybody is selling, and it's not looking good," said Nick Mokhoff, head of equities trading at Alliance-Menatep, adding shares were likely to fall further tomorrow.
But the Russian Trading System Index of 21 leading shares fell only 1.17 percent on $23.3 million trade, more than double Wednesday's volume.
Yuri Agaronik, head analyst at Prospekt investment company, said bid/ask spreads would double on Friday from Thursday's levels, the most significant indication of the market's caution.
Utility Irkutskenergo's spread had doubled to $0.0970/$0.1050 at Thursday's close from $0.1070/$0.1115 the day before.
Victor Pitaleff of Renaissance Capital speculated that as prices fell deals would dry up. "Big holders will not be able to sell," he said.
Terry Olin of Troika-Dialog said the market's first reaction was to slow trade by dropping bid prices, which guaranteed operators would not have stock dumped on them, rather than to shout "sell!".
"The initial reaction is to jump away from the bid... What we're seeing now is not happening on any volume. This should not carry past tomorrow morning," he said.
After Yeltsin's July 3 election run-off victory prices dropped sharply, when expected Western demand failed to materialise, but trade volume also fell at the time.

In recent weeks prices have been edging up, though Western investors have said the health of the 65-year-old Russian leader, who has rarely been seen in public since late June, was a major damper on prices.
On Thursday, shares had ticked down before 1300, when it was learned that Yeltsin had announced the operation during a television interview.
Mosenergo had fallen after two mid-day $2 million dollar deals, which Agaronik speculated were initiated by sellers, leading to the falling off.
Moscow Telephone (MGTS) jumped to $590.00 from $515.00, an indication of lack of liquidity rather than high demand, he said.
Rostelekom, which announced first half pre-tax profit of 1.38 trillion roubles, closed at $2.45 after falling to $2.62 at 1200 GMT from a previous close of $2.68.
Many traders said the market could fall until an announcement of the outcome of Yeltsin's operation, or news that the operation was not serious.
Some investors would jump in to pick up low-priced stocks, but few traders expected high volume sales, especially if prices dropped sharply.
"I think the market will not react very well to this," Pitaleff said. "But in the long term if the operation turns out well, it will turn out for the good."
